summary: This document describes the Segment Routing Replication segment, used for multipoint service delivery. It allows a packet to be copied at a replication node and sent to downstream nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: Some network services have to deliver one packet to many sites at once. This RFC adds a Segment Routing building block for that: a node with a replication segment makes one copy of the packet for each destination on its list and forwards each copy down its own path.

questions: what is an sr replication segment
subtitle: A Segment Routing building block that copies one packet at a node and sends the copies to several downstream nodes.

tldr.problem: Multipoint services such as Multicast VPN and Ethernet VPN need one packet delivered to many egress nodes, and Segment Routing had no standard way to say "copy this packet here and send the copies to these nodes".
tldr.mechanism: A Replication segment is a local segment at a replication node. Its Replication-SID selects a list of replication branches, and the node makes one copy per branch, using a label push in SR-MPLS or the new End.Replicate behavior in SRv6.
tldr.outcome: Replication segments can be used on their own for ingress replication, or stitched into trees by a control plane. The document also sets rules for the Hop Limit, ICMPv6 errors and ping, so that a replicated packet cannot be used to flood a node with error messages. The RFC is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9960.

today: RFC 9524 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2024. It has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9960. The document leaves the stitching of Replication segments into trees to other specifications, including the point-to-multipoint policy work.

sections.title: What a Replication Segment Does
sections.content:
A Replication segment is a new kind of segment for Segment Routing (SR), defined in RFC 8402. It lets a node, called a replication node, copy packets and send the copies to a set of other nodes, the downstream nodes, inside an SR domain. The downstream nodes may be directly connected, and a packet can be replicated to a node that is not adjacent without any state on the transit routers in between.

The document covers both data planes: Segment Routing with Multiprotocol Label Switching (SR-MPLS) in RFC 8660 and Segment Routing with IPv6 (SRv6) in RFC 8986.

The simplest use is a single Replication segment that holds the ingress node of a multipoint service and all its egress nodes as downstream nodes. That is what ingress replication, described in RFC 7988, has always done for Multicast VPN in RFC 6513 and for the broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast traffic of Ethernet VPN in RFC 7432. The segment can be provisioned by hand on each node or set up by an auto-discovery procedure. Replication segments can also be chained together to build trees, and the control plane for doing that, such as a path computation element with a point-to-multipoint policy, is left to other documents. Managing IP multicast groups, building multicast trees and multicast congestion control are all out of scope here.
sections.plainLanguage: The segment gives a node a list of destinations. When a packet arrives for that segment, the node makes one copy for each destination and sends each copy on its own way.

sections.title: The Replication Segment and Its State
sections.content:
A Replication segment is a local segment at a replication node, and it is identified by the tuple of a Replication-ID and a Node-ID. The Replication-ID is unique within the replication node, and the Node-ID is the address of that node. The Replication-ID is a variable-length field; in the simplest case it is a 32-bit number, and its length is set by whatever signalling mechanism programs the segment.

The segment has three elements. The Replication-SID is the identifier used in the forwarding plane, which is an SR-MPLS label or an SRv6 SID. The downstream nodes are the set of nodes to which packets are replicated. The replication state is what the node keeps for the segment, and it is a list of replication branches, which may be empty. Each branch is a pair of a downstream node and the Replication-SID of the segment at that node. How the replication node reaches the downstream node can be given as an interface or next hop for an adjacent node, as a Flexible Algorithm path, or as an explicit path made of a list of SIDs or a Segment Routing Policy.

A packet is steered into the segment in one of two ways: when the active segment is a locally instantiated Replication-SID, or when the root of a multipoint service does it by local configuration. Either way the packet is replicated to every downstream node in the state. A leaf node has a segment with the leaf role and an empty list, and its Replication-SID may identify the multipoint service. A bud node is both a replication node and a leaf, so its segment has both a list of branches and the leaf role.
sections.plainLanguage: Each segment has a name, an identifier used on the wire, and a list of branches. A branch says where to send a copy and which identifier the copy should carry when it arrives.

sections.title: The SR-MPLS Data Plane
sections.content:
When the active segment is a Replication-SID, the processing pops the incoming label and looks up the replication state. For each branch in that state, the node pushes the downstream Replication-SID, and an optional segment list, onto the packet, so that the copy is steered to the downstream node. At a leaf or bud node the operation on the incoming Replication-SID is NEXT, and delivery of the payload off the tree is decided by local configuration, which may involve looking at the next SID to get the context that is needed.

Several details are allowed in the label stack. SIDs may be placed before the downstream Replication-SID to guide a packet from a node that is not adjacent to the replication node. A replication node may replicate to a downstream node that is not adjacent by inserting SIDs in the copy in front of the downstream Replication-SID, and that downstream node may be a leaf, another replication node, or both in the case of a bud. A node may also use an Anycast-SID or a BGP PeerSet-SID to send a copy to one downstream replication node in a set of Anycast nodes, but only when every node in the set has an identical Replication-SID and reaches the same receivers. Finally, there may be SIDs after the Replication-SID, which the leaf and bud nodes use to forward the packet off the tree independently of the Replication-SID.
sections.plainLanguage: With MPLS labels, the node pops the label that named the segment and pushes a new label stack on each copy, with the label of the segment at the far end.

sections.title: SRv6 and the End.Replicate Behavior
sections.content:
For SRv6, this RFC defines a new endpoint behavior, End.Replicate, which is the endpoint behavior that replicates a packet and forwards the copies according to the replication state. The outer header is reused, and the downstream Replication-SID from the state is written into the destination address of the outer IPv6 header. Where a branch needs a particular path, H.Encaps.Red may be used with a segment list, and the penultimate segment of that encapsulation performs the Ultimate Segment Decapsulation flavor of End/End.X and forwards the inner packet to the downstream node. The operator has to make sure the path has room for the extra SRv6 encapsulation.

The Hop Limit has to be handled carefully. When a packet is processed at a local Replication-SID, the IPv6 Hop Limit must be decremented and must not be zero, or the packet is not replicated. A root node sets the Hop Limit by local policy, and that policy should set it so that a copy can still reach the furthest leaf. A node that forwards replicated packets on an IPv6 locator prefix can decrement the Hop Limit to zero and send ICMPv6 errors to the root, which can turn into a storm of error packets. A Replication segment therefore has an optional IPv6 Hop Limit Threshold, whose default is zero. If it is set, a replication node must discard an incoming packet with a local Replication-SID whose Hop Limit is below the threshold, and log that in a rate-limited way. The threshold should be set so that a packet can still be replicated to the furthest leaf.
sections.plainLanguage: With IPv6, the node copies the packet, puts the far end's identifier in the destination address of each copy, and forwards it. The Hop Limit is a safety net, so that a copy that has been going round in circles is dropped instead of being copied forever.

sections.title: Hop Limit, ICMPv6 Errors and Ping
sections.content:
Section 2.4 of RFC 4443 says that an ICMPv6 error message must not be sent as a result of receiving a packet addressed to an IPv6 multicast address, because replicated packets would otherwise overwhelm the source with errors. There are two exceptions: the Packet Too Big message used for Path MTU discovery, and the Parameter Problem message with Code 2 that reports an unrecognized IPv6 option. An implementation of a Replication segment for SRv6 must enforce the same restrictions and exceptions. A replication node therefore discards a packet whose Hop Limit is one or less, and does not send an ICMPv6 Time Exceeded message for it.

Ping needs care too. If the source knows the Replication-SID in advance, it can ping the Replication-SID of a leaf or bud node by putting it in the destination address, with or without a segment routing header, as the last segment. The source must compute the ICMPv6 Echo Request checksum using the Replication-SID of the leaf or bud node as the destination address. The packet can be sent to a transit node's Replication-SID: the transit node replicates it, replacing the destination address, until it reaches the leaf or bud node, which answers with an Echo Reply. A transit node may also replicate the Echo Request to other leaves, and those nodes drop it because the checksum no longer matches. Traceroute to a leaf or bud node is not possible, because the Time Exceeded message is not allowed for a Replication-SID.
sections.plainLanguage: Replicated packets must not trigger error messages, or one source could be flooded with them. A ping can still reach a leaf, but the checksum has to be worked out for the leaf's identifier in advance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An SR domain has to be protected from outside attackers. In SR-MPLS, MPLS should be disabled on the external interfaces of edge nodes, or labeled traffic should be filtered there. In SRv6, all the SIDs should be allocated from one prefix block, and every external interface should have an inbound infrastructure access control list that drops packets with a destination in that block. Nodes that provision SIDs can also drop packets addressed to their own local SIDs unless the source address is in the operator's own prefix, and traffic with spoofed source addresses should be denied as recommended in BCP 84. The block used for SIDs may be an address that is not globally routable.

Without these protections, an attacker from outside the domain can send packets that use the replication services inside it. Because a Replication segment tree always ends at a leaf or bud node, where the packet is decapsulated, an attacker cannot use a stack of Replication segments for amplification or link exhaustion, but can inject traffic to the receivers of the service.

Bad provisioning can also make a chain of Replication segments loop. Without a control plane, replicated packets can storm until the MPLS TTL or the IPv6 Hop Limit reaches zero, and a control plane such as a path computation element can prevent that. Finally, the exception for the ICMPv6 Parameter Problem message with Code 2 is a hole: an attacker who sends a packet to a Replication-SID with the source address of a node, and with an extension header that has an unknown mandatory option, can cause a flood of Parameter Problem messages against that source. The Hop Limit Threshold check helps to limit that.
sections.plainLanguage: Only nodes inside the network should be able to use the replication service, so the edges of the domain have to filter packets with these identifiers. Poor configuration can also make copies circle forever, and the Hop Limit check limits the damage.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
Appendix A works through one example in both data planes. The topology has a replication node R1 whose segment has three downstream nodes, R2, R6 and R7. R1 is directly connected to R2, so the copy for R2 carries only the label of R2's segment, and R2, acting as a leaf, pops it and delivers the payload. The copy for R6 is steered along the shortest path using R6's node identifier, and the copy for R7 is steered through R4 using R4's node identifier and an adjacency identifier from R4 to R7. Nodes R3, R4 and R5 have no Replication segment of their own; they only forward the copies.

The SRv6 version uses the same shape with IPv6 addresses. A node k has a local SID space, and the SID bound to the End.Replicate function is 2001:db8:cccc:k:Fk::/128. R1 builds one encapsulated copy for each downstream node, and for R7 it either encapsulates twice or, because it is the root, combines the two encapsulations into one.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows one node making three copies, each steered to a different destination, with two of the copies passing over nodes that do nothing but forward them.
